links.outcome: LLM output changes under counterfactual patient demographic edits versus a paraphrase baseline
links.effect: MedQA gender-swap flip rate 14.9% vs paraphrase flip rate 14.1% (indistinguishable); MedPerturb demographic and style effects mostly vanish, with 5 of 120 tests significant after baseline correction.
links.quote: We find that these effects largely dissipate when we account for general model sensitivity, with only 5 of 120 tests reaching statistical significance.

links.outcome: Prediction flips on medical QA under meaning-preserving paraphrase of inputs
links.effect: Paraphrasing inputs alone induced prediction flip rates of 14.1% on MedQA, similar to the 14.9% from changing patient gender.
links.quote: However, this is statistically indistinguishable from the flip rates induced by simply paraphrasing inputs (14.1%).

unlisted_practices: Compare counterfactual-edit effects against a paraphrase (meaning-preserving) baseline using statistical testing before attributing LLM sensitivity to a targeted factor
Use per-sample and regression metrics rather than only aggregate flip rates to evaluate counterfactual effects

screen.reason: Empirical evaluation of LLM bias and robustness benchmarks (MedQA, MedPerturb) introducing a baseline methodology for counterfactual prompting evaluations.
